When filming the mind-bending climactic sequence where Cooper is trapped inside the fifth-dimensional Tesseract and desperately tries to send the Morse code message “S-T-A-Y” to his daughter, director Christopher Nolan famously refused to rely entirely on a green screen. Instead, the production team built a massive, intensely complex physical set. Designed to visually represent time as a physical, navigable dimension, the set was a three-story practical labyrinth modeled after slit-scan photography. Matthew McConaughey was suspended in a highly complicated wire rig, allowing him to actually float through the massive physical structure and tangibly interact with the “strings” of gravity. By forcing the actor to physically maneuver through a real, constructed space, Nolan grounded one of the most abstract sci-fi concepts of the decade in a deeply human, tactile performance.

Interstellar (2014), directed by Christopher Nolan, starring Matthew McConaughey, Anne Hathaway, Jessica Chastain, Michael Caine. As Earth faces a devastating global blight and inevitable extinction, a former NASA pilot leads a desperate, last-ditch mission through a newly discovered wormhole to find a habitable new home for humanity among the stars.
